sections.text:
**Exploring current recommendations**

I think we need to stay updated with current recommendations, maybe through web searches. I realize that AI search engines often provide insights on SEO and GEO, which are constantly changing. There’s so much information out there! I should consider browsing to get the latest details, so I can deliver accurate and relevant recommendations. It's all about making sure I'm providing the best information for the user’s needs.

To get your website cited by AI search engines — ChatGPT Search, Google AI Overviews / AI Mode, Perplexity, Bing Copilot, etc. — think less “trick the AI” and more **make your pages easy to crawl, trust, extract, and cite**.

There’s no guaranteed submission form that forces citations. The practical playbook is:

## 1. Make sure AI/search crawlers can access your site

If your content is blocked, it won’t be cited.

Check your `robots.txt` and CDN/WAF rules for:

- **Googlebot** — for Google Search and AI features.
- **Bingbot** — important for Bing Copilot and Microsoft AI experiences.
- **OAI-SearchBot** — OpenAI’s search crawler for ChatGPT search results.
- Avoid accidentally blocking crawlers with Cloudflare, bot protection, geo blocking, paywalls, login walls, or heavy JavaScript rendering.

OpenAI says publishers that allow **OAI-SearchBot** can appear in ChatGPT search results and track referral traffic from ChatGPT; it also distinguishes that from **GPTBot**, which relates to training opt-out controls. ([help-lb.openai.com](https://help-lb.openai.com/en/articles/12627856-publishers-and-developers-faq?utm_source=openai))

## 2. Do strong traditional SEO first

AI search engines still rely heavily on web search indexes, retrieval systems, and rankings. Google’s own guidance says SEO best practices remain relevant for AI features like AI Overviews and AI Mode. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features?utm_source=openai))

Prioritize:

- Fast, crawlable pages.
- Clean internal linking.
- Descriptive titles and meta descriptions.
- XML sitemap.
- Canonical tags.
- Helpful, original content.
- Good Core Web Vitals.
- HTTPS.
- No indexation mistakes.
- Clear page hierarchy: `h1`, `h2`, `h3`.

If you are not ranking in normal search, you are much less likely to be cited in AI answers.

## 3. Create “answer-ready” pages

AI systems often cite sources that can directly support a specific claim. So each important page should have:

- A clear question or topic in the heading.
- A concise answer near the top.
- Supporting details below.
- Definitions, steps, tables, examples, pros/cons, FAQs.
- Specific facts, dates, numbers, comparisons, and methodology.
- Original insight instead of generic rewritten content.

Example structure:

```text
H1: Best CRM for Small Law Firms in 2026

Short answer:
The best CRM for most small law firms is X because...

Comparison table:
Product | Best for | Pricing | Key limitation

Detailed sections:
- Why X is best overall
- Best low-cost option
- Best for intake automation
- How we evaluated these CRMs
- FAQs
```

AI search engines need extractable passages. Don’t bury the answer after 1,500 words of intro.

## 4. Publish content that deserves to be cited

Generic blog posts are rarely citation-worthy. AI engines are more likely to cite pages that add something useful, such as:

- Original research.
- First-party data.
- Benchmarks.
- Case studies.
- Product comparisons.
- Pricing breakdowns.
- Expert commentary.
- Step-by-step procedures.
- Local or niche information not widely available elsewhere.
- Clear explanations of complex topics.

A good test: **If an AI answer cited your page, what unique claim would your page support?**

If the answer is “nothing unique,” improve the page.

## 5. Build topical authority, not just individual posts

AI search engines tend to favor sources that look authoritative for a topic. Build clusters around your niche.

For example, if you sell accounting software for contractors, don’t publish only:

- “Best Accounting Software”

Also publish:

- “Accounting Software for General Contractors”
- “Job Costing vs. Project Accounting”
- “How Contractors Track Retainage”
- “Construction WIP Reports Explained”
- “QuickBooks vs. X for Contractors”
- “Chart of Accounts for Construction Companies”
- “Construction Accounting Glossary”

Then internally link them together.

## 6. Use structured data, but don’t overestimate it

Schema helps search engines understand your pages, but it is not a magic “get cited by AI” switch. Google says structured data should match visible page content and follow its guidelines. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features?utm_source=openai)) Google also notes there is no special schema markup required for generative AI search features. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide?authuser=4&hl=en&utm_source=openai))

Useful schema types include:

- `Article`
- `FAQPage`
- `HowTo`
- `Product`
- `Review`
- `Organization`
- `Person`
- `LocalBusiness`
- `BreadcrumbList`
- `SoftwareApplication`
- `Dataset`

But the visible content matters more than markup alone.

## 7. Make your brand/entity easy to understand

AI engines cite brands they can contextualize. Make sure your site clearly states:

- Who you are.
- What you do.
- Who your content is for.
- Who wrote or reviewed the content.
- Credentials.
- Contact information.
- Editorial standards.
- About page.
- Author bios.
- Company location, if relevant.
- SameAs links to authoritative profiles.

For YMYL topics — health, finance, legal, safety — expertise and trust signals matter even more.

## 8. Earn mentions and citations from other reputable sites

AI systems often triangulate across the web. Your own site matters, but so do third-party references.

Work on getting mentioned in:

- Industry publications.
- Comparison sites.
- Review platforms.
- Podcasts.
- Reddit/community discussions, where appropriate.
- YouTube descriptions/transcripts.
- Wikipedia/Wikidata, if genuinely notable.
- Local directories.
- Academic or government sources, if relevant.
- Partner/customer case studies.

The goal is for the web to consistently associate your brand with your topic.

## 9. Keep important pages fresh

AI search is often used for current answers. Add visible:

- Published date.
- Updated date.
- Version history, where useful.
- Current pricing or availability.
- “Last reviewed by” for expert content.

Do not fake freshness, but do maintain pages that target changing topics.

## 10. Optimize for specific prompts, not just keywords

Traditional SEO asks: “What keyword do I want to rank for?”

AI citation optimization asks: “What question would someone ask an AI where my page should be cited?”

Examples:

- “What is the best payroll software for restaurants?”
- “How do I calculate customer churn?”
- “Is X better than Y for Shopify stores?”
- “What are the OSHA requirements for small construction companies?”
- “How much does a fractional CFO cost?”

Create pages that answer these directly.

## 11. Make pages technically easy to extract

Avoid making your most important content hard for crawlers or AI retrieval systems to parse.

Do:

- Use semantic HTML.
- Put key answers in plain text.
- Use tables where useful.
- Add alt text to important images.
- Include transcripts for videos.
- Avoid putting important copy only in images, PDFs, accordions, tabs, or scripts.
- Make sure server-rendered HTML contains the main content.

AI engines need to pull passages cleanly.

## 12. Monitor AI visibility

You can’t fully track all AI citations yet, but you can monitor signals.

Use:

- Google Search Console.
- Bing Webmaster Tools.
- Bing’s AI Performance report, which shows how a site’s content is used in AI-generated answers across Microsoft Copilot and partner experiences, including cited URLs and grounding queries. ([bing.com](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/ai-performance-9f8e7d6c?utm_source=openai))
- Server logs for AI/search crawler visits.
- Analytics referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot, Gemini, etc.
- Manual testing of priority prompts.
- Brand monitoring tools.

Track prompts like:

```text
best [category] for [audience]
how to [solve problem]
[brand] vs [competitor]
what is the cost of [service]
top [tools/products] for [use case]
```

## 13. Don’t rely on “LLMs.txt” alone

Some people recommend adding an `llms.txt` file. It may be useful as an experimental content map, but it is not an official standard across major AI search engines, and it will not compensate for weak content, poor crawling, or lack of authority.

If you add one, treat it as optional, not core strategy.

## 14. Use a practical page template

For pages you want AI engines to cite, use this structure:

```text
Title:
Clear query-focused title

Intro:
2–4 sentence direct answer

Key facts:
Bullet list of the most citation-worthy claims

Main explanation:
Detailed, well-sourced content

Comparison table:
If relevant

Methodology:
How you know what you know

Examples:
Concrete use cases

FAQ:
Short answers to related questions

Author/reviewer:
Credentials and date updated
```

## 15. Avoid spammy “GEO” tactics

Be careful with agencies promising guaranteed AI citations. Google’s guidance emphasizes helpful content, crawlability, user experience, and standard SEO fundamentals for AI features, not secret AI-specific markup. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/05/succeeding-in-ai-search?utm_source=openai))

Avoid:

- Mass-producing thin AI content.
